title: Names, Ranks and Roles
bigQuestion: When the Bible names heavenly beings, is it describing what they are, what they do, or where they stand?

story.title: Holy, Holy, Holy
story.kicker: In the year a king died, the prophet Isaiah says he saw the LORD enthroned, with burning beings calling out above him.
paragraphs: Isaiah 6 opens with a date. "In the year that king Uzziah died," Isaiah says, he saw the LORD sitting on a throne, high and lifted up. Uzziah had ruled Judah for decades, and his death is usually dated around 740 BCE. A long reign had ended. The prophet's vision begins at a moment of change for his people.

In the vision, the hem of the LORD's robe fills the temple. Above him stand seraphim. Each has six wings. With two they cover their faces, with two they cover their feet, and with two they fly. They call to one another: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." The doorposts shake, and the house fills with smoke.

Isaiah does not feel ready. He is shaken. He says he is a man of unclean lips, living among a people of unclean lips. Then one of the seraphim flies to him with a live coal from the altar. It touches his mouth, and the seraph tells him his guilt is taken away. The scene moves from fear to cleansing.

Then a voice asks, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Isaiah answers, "Here am I; send me." Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible, read the word "us" as God speaking in front of his heavenly council. Other readers hear a royal way of speaking, or, in many Christian readings, a hint of the Trinity.

The seraphim's song did not stay in Isaiah's book. Jewish prayer services still repeat it in a prayer called the Kedushah. Many Christian services sing it in the Sanctus. In this chapter you will look closely at the names the Bible gives to heavenly beings like these, and at what those names tell you.
story.think: The seraphim cover their faces even while standing near God. What might that detail be meant to show a reader about them?

lessons.title: Angel Is a Job Title
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew and Greek words for angel mean messenger, so Heiser read angel as a job description, not a kind of being.
reading: Open Genesis 32. In verse 1, Jacob is traveling, and "the angels of God" meet him. Two verses later, Jacob sends "messengers" ahead to his brother Esau. English uses two different words. The Hebrew uses one word both times: *mal'ak*, plural mal'akim. Jacob's messengers were ordinary men. The beings who met him were from God. The word is the same because both groups do the same task. They carry a message.

Greek works the same way. The New Testament word is *angelos*, and it too means messenger. Mark 1:2 uses it for John the Baptist, a human being. The last book of the Old Testament is called Malachi, which means "my messenger" in Hebrew. So when readers see "angel" in an English Bible, the older languages are usually saying "one who is sent." Translators decide from the context whether the messenger is human or heavenly.

Heiser built on this point in his book Angels (2018). He argued that many biblical terms describe a being's role, while others describe its status or its home. Angel, in his reading, is a role word. It tells you what a being is doing, not what kind of being it is. This helps explain why the Bible can call the same figure an angel in one verse and something else in the next. Other scholars make the same language point, even when they read particular passages differently.

words.d: Hebrew for messenger; used for both human and heavenly messengers
Greek for messenger; the source of the English word angel
a term that names what a being does, such as messenger, rather than what it is

look.title: One Word, Two Kinds of Messenger
look.text: Genesis 32:1: Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him. Genesis 32:3: Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to Esau his brother. In Hebrew, "angels" and "messengers" here are the same word, mal'akim.
look.prompt: If you only had the Hebrew word, how would you decide which messengers were human and which were heavenly? What clues in each verse help?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word mal'ak mean?
check.why: Mal'ak means messenger. Genesis 32 uses it for heavenly beings and for Jacob's human messengers.

check.q: Why does Genesis 32 use the same Hebrew word for God's angels and Jacob's messengers?
choices: Because Jacob's messengers were secretly angels
Because the Hebrew language had only one word for any person
Because both groups carry out the same task of bringing a message
Because the verse was copied wrongly
check.why: The word names a task. Both groups are sent with a message, so both are mal'akim.

check.q: In Angels (2018), how did Heiser describe the word angel?
choices: As a word for a being's role or job
As the highest rank of heavenly being
As a word used only in the New Testament
As a name for people who have died
check.why: Heiser treated angel as a role word. It tells what a being does, carrying messages, not what kind of being it is.

lessons.title: Elohim, Sons of God, Holy Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read elohim, sons of God and holy ones as status words that place beings in the unseen realm around God.
reading: Psalm 82:1 reads, in the King James Version, "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods." In Hebrew, both "God" and "gods" are the same word: *elohim*. Heiser argued that elohim is not a name for one particular being. It is a word for any being whose natural home is the spirit world. The God of Israel is called elohim. So are the members of his council. So, once, is the spirit of the dead Samuel in 1 Samuel 28:13.

Another phrase is *sons of God*. In Job 1:6 and 2:1 the sons of God come to present themselves before the LORD. In Job 38:7 they shout for joy when the earth's foundations are laid. Heiser read "son" here as a family and household term. It marks beings who belong to God's heavenly household. Many other readers agree these are heavenly beings in Job. Genesis 6, where the phrase also appears, is more debated, and later units treat it.

A third term is *holy ones*, in Hebrew qedoshim. Psalm 89:5 to 7 speaks of an assembly of the holy ones in the heavens. It asks who among the heavenly beings can compare to the LORD. Holy means set apart. For Heiser, all three terms describe status: where a being belongs and how it stands near God. They say little about what job it is doing at a given moment. That is what role words like messenger do.

words.d: Hebrew word used for God, for the gods of the council and for other beings of the spirit world
a phrase in Job and elsewhere for heavenly beings in God's household
Hebrew qedoshim; heavenly beings set apart, gathered in God's assembly
a term that says where a being belongs or how it ranks, not what task it is doing

look.title: The Assembly of the Holy Ones
look.text: "For who in the heaven can be compared unto the LORD? who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the LORD? God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him."
look.prompt: The word translated "saints" here is qedoshim, holy ones. Who does the psalm say is in this assembly, and where is it?

check.q: In Psalm 82:1, which Hebrew word is translated both "God" and "gods"?
check.why: Psalm 82:1 uses elohim for the God of Israel and for the members of his council.

check.q: According to Heiser, what does the word elohim mark?
choices: A being whose natural home is the spirit world
check.why: Heiser argued elohim is a word for any being of the spirit world, which is why it can name God, the council and even Samuel's spirit.

check.q: In Job 38:7, what do the sons of God do?
choices: They shout for joy as the earth is founded
They guard the garden of Eden
They carry the ark of the covenant
check.why: Job 38:7 says the morning stars sang together and the sons of God shouted for joy when the earth's foundations were laid.

lessons.title: Host, Ministers and Watchers
lessons.mainIdea: Host, ministers and watchers name the heavenly beings as an army, as servants and as those who keep watch.
reading: In 1 Kings 22:19 the prophet Micaiah says he saw the LORD on his throne with "all the host of heaven" standing on his right and his left. *Host* translates the Hebrew tsaba, a word for an army. The title "LORD of hosts" appears hundreds of times in the Hebrew Bible. Isaiah's seraphim use it. In Luke 2:13 a "multitude of the heavenly host" praises God over the shepherds. The picture is of a great, ordered company around a king.

Psalm 103:20 to 21 calls on the angels and hosts to bless the LORD. It calls them "ministers of his, that do his pleasure." *Ministers* here means servants who attend a king. Psalm 104:4 says God makes his ministers a flaming fire, and Hebrews 1:7 quotes that verse. These words describe what the heavenly beings do. They serve and carry out orders, which fits Heiser's idea of role words.

Daniel 4 adds an unusual term. King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of "a watcher and an holy one" coming down from heaven (4:13). A decision is said to come "by the decree of the watchers" (4:17). This part of Daniel is in Aramaic, and the word is 'ir, plural 'irin, meaning one who is awake. The Watchers in Daniel are God's faithful servants. The same word is used in the Aramaic copies of 1 Enoch for the Watchers who sinned. Heiser noted that the term by itself does not mean good or bad.

words.d: from Hebrew tsaba, an army; the whole company of heavenly beings around God
servants who attend a king; used for heavenly beings in Psalms 103 and 104
Aramaic 'ir, one who is awake; a heavenly being in Daniel 4 and in 1 Enoch

look.title: The Decree of the Watchers
look.text: "This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will."
look.prompt: The watchers and holy ones announce a decision here. According to the verse, who really rules, and what are the watchers doing?

check.q: The Hebrew word tsaba, translated "host," first of all means what?
check.why: Tsaba is a word for an army. "LORD of hosts" pictures God as commander of a heavenly company.

check.q: In which book does a watcher and a holy one come down from heaven in a king's dream?
check.why: Daniel 4:13 tells of Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a watcher and a holy one coming down from heaven.

check.q: What did Heiser note about the word watcher?
choices: It always means a fallen being
It is only used in the New Testament
It is another word for a human prophet
By itself it does not mean good or bad
check.why: The watchers of Daniel 4 are faithful. 1 Enoch uses the same word for Watchers who sinned. The word itself is neutral.

lessons.title: Cherubim
lessons.mainIdea: Cherubim in the Bible are guardians of God's presence, not the chubby babies of later art.
reading: The first *cherubim* in the Bible stand at the east of Eden in Genesis 3:24. They guard the way to the tree of life with a flaming sword. In Exodus 25:18 to 22, two golden cherubim are made for the cover of the ark of the covenant. Their wings stretch over it. God says he will meet Moses and speak with him from between them. In both places, cherubim guard the space where God is present.

Ezekiel 1 describes four living creatures beneath a throne-chariot. Each has four faces and four wings. In Ezekiel 10:20 the prophet says he knew these were cherubim. Many scholars compare them to the winged guardian figures of the ancient Near East. The Assyrian kings, for example, set huge winged creatures with human heads at their palace gates. Heiser read the biblical cherubim in this setting. They are throne guardians around a divine king.

Later art changed the picture. Renaissance painters filled their works with winged baby figures, called *putti*, borrowed from the cupids of Greek and Roman art. Over time people began calling these babies cherubs. Heiser and many others point out that nothing in Genesis, Exodus or Ezekiel describes cherubim as babies. The texts describe powerful, many-faced beings who guard what is holy.

words.d: Hebrew plural of cherub; winged beings who guard God's presence in Genesis, Exodus and Ezekiel
a being who stands at or beside a king's throne to guard it
winged baby figures in Renaissance art, borrowed from classical cupids

look.title: Three Places Cherubim Stand
look.text: Genesis 3:24: cherubim with a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life. Exodus 25:22: God will speak to Moses from between the two cherubim on the ark. Ezekiel 10:20: the living creatures under God's throne are cherubim.
look.prompt: What do these three places have in common? Write one sentence that describes the job of cherubim across all three texts.

check.q: Where do cherubim first appear in the Bible?
choices: Guarding the way to the tree of life in Genesis 3:24
At the empty tomb in Matthew 28
check.why: Genesis 3:24 places cherubim east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life.

check.q: In Exodus 25, where are the golden cherubim placed?
choices: At the gates of the city
On the cover of the ark of the covenant
At the top of Mount Sinai
check.why: Exodus 25:18-22 places two golden cherubim on the ark's cover, with God speaking from between them.

check.q: Where did the picture of cherubs as winged babies come from?
choices: Renaissance art that borrowed classical cupids
check.why: Renaissance putti were modeled on classical cupids. The biblical texts describe powerful guardians, not babies.

lessons.title: Seraphim
lessons.mainIdea: Seraphim, the burning ones of Isaiah 6, stand above God's throne and call out his holiness.
reading: Isaiah 6 is the only place in the Bible where *seraphim* appear clearly as heavenly beings. They stand above the LORD's throne. Each has six wings. They cover their faces and feet and call out, "Holy, holy, holy." One of them brings a coal from the altar to cleanse Isaiah's lips. They are worshipers and also agents who act.

The Hebrew root saraph is linked to burning. So seraphim can be translated "burning ones." Many readers take this as a picture of fiery brightness around God. But the same word appears elsewhere for serpents. In Numbers 21:6 the LORD sends "fiery serpents" among the people, and the Hebrew there is seraphim. Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6 mention a flying saraph.

Heiser noted this link. He argued that the seraphim may have been pictured as shining, serpent-like throne guardians. Egyptian royal art often shows cobras, called *uraeus* serpents, guarding a king. Other scholars prefer to keep the image simpler, as glowing beings with human-like faces, feet and hands. The text of Isaiah 6 gives faces, feet and wings, and leaves the rest to the reader.

words.d: Hebrew plural of seraph, burning ones; the six-winged beings above God's throne in Isaiah 6
Hebrew root linked to burning; also used for serpents in Numbers 21 and Isaiah
the upright cobra shown guarding Egyptian kings in ancient art

look.title: Wings in the Throne Visions
look.prompt: Which text's creatures look most like Isaiah's seraphim by wing count? What else might Revelation 4 borrow from Isaiah 6?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word seraphim most likely mean?
check.why: Seraphim comes from a root linked to burning, so it is often translated burning ones.

check.q: Where else does the Hebrew word seraphim appear, used for serpents?
check.why: Numbers 21:6 calls the snakes sent among the people seraphim, fiery serpents.

check.q: How did Heiser's reading of the seraphim differ from a simpler reading?
choices: He said they were human priests
He said they had no wings
He suggested they were pictured as serpent-like throne guardians
He said Isaiah 6 was about Egypt
check.why: Heiser pointed to the serpent meaning of saraph and to Egyptian cobra guardians. Other scholars picture glowing beings with human features.

lessons.title: Living Creatures in Revelation
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 4 draws on both Ezekiel and Isaiah for its four living creatures around God's throne.
reading: In Revelation 4:6 to 8, John sees four *living creatures* around God's throne. One is like a lion, one like a calf, one has a face like a man, and one is like a flying eagle. Each has six wings and is full of eyes. Day and night they say, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come."

Readers who know the Hebrew Bible notice the echoes. The four faces of lion, ox, man and eagle come from Ezekiel 1:10, where each creature has all four. The six wings and the triple "holy" come from Isaiah 6. Revelation blends the two visions into one scene. This kind of borrowing is called *allusion*. A writer brings in older texts so that readers will recall them.

Heiser read Revelation 4 as another picture of God's throne room, with the same council setting found in the prophets. Christian tradition from about the late 100s onward also linked the four faces to the four Gospels. Irenaeus made one such pairing, and later writers made others. That later link is a reading of the symbols, not something Revelation itself states.

words.d: the four beings around God's throne in Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4
a brief reference that calls an earlier text to the reader's mind
the scene of God seated as king, surrounded by heavenly beings

look.title: Two Visions Blended
look.text: Ezekiel 1: four creatures, each with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle) and four wings. Isaiah 6: seraphim with six wings calling "Holy, holy, holy." Revelation 4: four creatures, each with one face (lion, calf, man, eagle), six wings, calling "Holy, holy, holy."
look.prompt: List two details Revelation takes from Ezekiel and two it takes from Isaiah. Why might John's vision bring both older visions together?

check.q: How many wings does each living creature have in Revelation 4:8?
check.why: Revelation 4:8 gives each creature six wings, like the seraphim of Isaiah 6.

check.q: Which older text supplies the four faces of lion, ox, man and eagle?
check.why: Ezekiel 1:10 gives each living creature the faces of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle.

check.q: Linking the four faces to the four Gospels is best described as what?
choices: A later Christian reading of the symbols
A rule from the Dead Sea Scrolls
check.why: Irenaeus and later writers made the Gospel pairings. Revelation itself does not state them.

sections.title: Ranks in the Text and Beyond

lessons.title: Archangels and Named Angels
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible uses the word archangel only twice, and names very few angels, but later Jewish writings name more.
reading: The word *archangel* means chief angel. It appears only twice in the New Testament. 1 Thessalonians 4:16 says the Lord will come down "with the voice of the archangel." Jude 9 calls Michael "the archangel" and tells of his dispute with the devil over the body of Moses. In Daniel 10:13 Michael is "one of the chief princes," and in Daniel 12:1 he is "the great prince" who stands for Daniel's people.

Only two angels are named in the Protestant Bible. Michael appears in Daniel, Jude and Revelation 12:7. *Gabriel* explains visions to Daniel in Daniel 8 and 9. In Luke 1 he announces the births of John and Jesus. The book of Tobit, which is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, names Raphael. There he calls himself one of seven holy angels who stand before God (12:15).

Jewish writings from the Second Temple period name more. 1 Enoch 20, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, lists holy angels who watch. They include Uriel, Raphael, Michael and Gabriel. Heiser read these lists as later developments of hints in the Bible, such as Daniel's chief princes. He urged readers to notice the difference between what the canonical texts say and what later writers added.

words.d: chief angel; used in the New Testament only in 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Jude 9
the angel called a chief prince in Daniel and the archangel in Jude 9
the angel who explains visions to Daniel and announces births in Luke 1
the era of the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, about 516 BCE to 70 CE

look.title: Angels Named in the Protestant Bible
look.cite: Michael: Daniel 10:13, 10:21, 12:1; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7. Gabriel: Daniel 8:16, 9:21; Luke 1:19, 1:26
look.prompt: Raphael and Uriel are well known today. Where do their names come from, if not from the Protestant Bible?

check.q: Which New Testament verse calls Michael the archangel?
check.why: Jude 9 names "Michael the archangel" disputing with the devil about the body of Moses.

check.q: In which book does Raphael call himself one of seven holy angels?
check.why: Tobit 12:15 has Raphael say he is one of the seven holy angels. Tobit is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

check.q: What does Daniel 10:13 call Michael?
check.why: Daniel 10:13 calls Michael one of the chief princes, a hint of rank that later writers built on.

lessons.title: Nine Choirs: A Later System
lessons.mainIdea: Paul's words for powers hint at ranks, but the nine choirs of angels come from a writer about 500 CE.
reading: Colossians 1:16 says that all things were created through Christ, "whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers." Ephesians 1:21 lists principality, power, might and dominion. These are words for rulers and their territories. Heiser argued that Paul used them for heavenly powers with authority over places and peoples. Paul does not arrange them into a ladder.

About 500 CE a Christian writer produced a book called The Celestial Hierarchy. He wrote under the name of Dionysius, a man Paul met in Athens (Acts 17:34). Scholars call him *Pseudo-Dionysius*, since the real author lived centuries later. He arranged angels into nine orders, often called the nine *choirs*, in three groups of three. Seraphim, cherubim and thrones came first. Dominions, powers and authorities came next. Principalities, archangels and angels came last. Translations name the middle group in slightly different ways.

This system shaped later thought. Thomas Aquinas discussed it, and Dante's Paradiso pictures the nine orders circling God. Catholic and Orthodox traditions still use it. Many Protestant readers see it as a thoughtful guess that goes beyond the text. Heiser's approach was to start with the terms in the Bible and to mark the full ranking as a later *hierarchy* built on them.

words.d: rulers; one of Paul's words for heavenly powers in Colossians and Ephesians
the unknown author, about 500 CE, of The Celestial Hierarchy, writing under an earlier name
the nine orders of angels in Pseudo-Dionysius's system
a system that ranks members from highest to lowest

look.title: Text and System Side by Side
look.text: Colossians 1:16 names four kinds of powers: thrones, dominions, principalities, powers. Pseudo-Dionysius, about 500 CE, lists nine orders in three groups: seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, powers, authorities; principalities, archangels, angels.
look.prompt: Which names in the nine choirs come from Paul, and which come from other Bible books? What did Pseudo-Dionysius add that neither source states?

check.q: About when did Pseudo-Dionysius write The Celestial Hierarchy?
check.why: The Celestial Hierarchy is dated to about 500 CE, centuries after the real Dionysius of Acts 17.

check.q: How did Heiser read Paul's words thrones, dominions, principalities and powers?
choices: As names for human church leaders
As the nine choirs in order
As words for heavenly powers with authority over places and peoples
As other names for the Watchers of Daniel 4
check.why: Heiser read them as rulership terms for heavenly powers over territories. Paul does not rank them.

check.q: Why is the author called Pseudo-Dionysius?
choices: He wrote under the name of a much earlier figure from Acts 17
check.why: He wrote as Dionysius, whom Paul met in Athens, but lived centuries later. Pseudo means false name.

lessons.title: Guardian Angels?
lessons.mainIdea: A few verses link angels to believers, and traditions differ on how far to take the idea of a personal guardian.
reading: In Matthew 18:10 Jesus says not to despise "these little ones," because "in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father." In Acts 12, Peter is freed from prison and knocks at the door of Mary's house. A servant named Rhoda runs to tell the others. They answer, "It is his angel" (12:15). Psalm 91:11 says God will give his angels charge over the one who trusts him.

Many Christians read these verses as teaching *guardian angels*. The Catholic Church teaches that each believer has an angel as protector and keeps a feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2. Jewish tradition has its own form of the idea. The Talmud (Shabbat 119b) tells of two ministering angels who walk a person home on the eve of the Sabbath. The Sabbath song Shalom Aleichem greets them.

Heiser encouraged readers to separate what these verses say from what later teaching builds on them. Matthew 18:10 says the little ones have angels who see God's face. It does not say how many angels or what they do. Acts 12:15 tells what Peter's friends believed. It is a report of their words, not a separate teaching. Careful readers weigh each verse on its own before building a doctrine.

words.d: an angel believed to watch over a particular person
a large collection of Jewish legal and teaching discussions, completed about 500 to 600 CE
a teaching that a religious community holds and passes on

look.title: Their Angels in Heaven
look.text: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven."
look.prompt: What exactly does this verse say about the little ones' angels? Make two lists: what the verse states, and what readers have added.

check.q: In Acts 12:15, who do Peter's friends think is at the door?
check.why: When Rhoda says Peter is at the door, the others answer, "It is his angel."

check.q: Which tradition keeps a feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2?
check.why: The Catholic Church teaches that each believer has a guardian angel and keeps a feast for them on October 2.

check.q: What does Matthew 18:10 say the little ones' angels do?
choices: Always see the face of the Father in heaven
Carry them to heaven when they die
check.why: The verse says their angels always behold the face of the Father. It says nothing further about their tasks.

lessons.title: People Do Not Become Angels
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser stressed that in the Bible angels and humans are different kinds of beings, and the dead do not become angels.
reading: In the 1946 film It's a Wonderful Life, a man who died long ago returns as Clarence, "Angel, Second Class," trying to earn his wings. Many people today say that someone who has died has become an angel. Heiser pointed out that this is a popular idea, not a biblical one. In the Bible, angels and humans are different kinds of beings.

Several texts support his point. Job 38:7 has the sons of God shouting for joy when the earth was founded, before any humans existed. In Matthew 22:30 Jesus says the raised dead will be "as the angels" in not marrying. The word as makes a comparison. It does not say they become angels. Hebrews 12:22 to 23 lists "an innumerable company of angels" and, separately, "the spirits of just men made perfect." The two groups stand side by side.

Heiser also drew on 1 Corinthians 6:3, where Paul says believers will judge angels. In his reading, the New Testament pictures redeemed humans raised to share in God's rule, as humans, even above the angels. Other Christian readers stress different parts of these texts, but most agree on the basic *distinction* between human and angel. The popular idea often grows from grief and love for someone who has died.

words.d: a clear difference between two things
being raised from death to a new bodily life, as the New Testament describes it
a belief widely held in a culture that may not come from the source texts

look.title: "As the Angels"
look.text: Matthew 22:30: in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven. Hebrews 12:22-23: the heavenly Jerusalem holds an innumerable company of angels, the church of the firstborn, God the Judge of all, and the spirits of just men made perfect.
look.prompt: Does either text say that people become angels? Point to the exact words that show how the writer compares or separates the two.

check.q: Which verse has the sons of God shouting for joy before humans existed?
check.why: Job 38:7 places the sons of God at the founding of the earth, before people were made.

check.q: In Matthew 22:30, what does Jesus say about the raised dead?
choices: They are as the angels in not marrying
check.why: Jesus compares them to angels in one way, not marrying. The word as makes a comparison, not a change of kind.

check.q: How does Hebrews 12:22-23 support Heiser's point?
choices: It lists angels and the spirits of just men as separate groups
It says angels were once humans
It names Michael as a human prophet
It says the dead earn wings
check.why: Hebrews 12:22-23 names the company of angels and the spirits of just men side by side, as two groups.

lessons.title: The Son Above the Angels
lessons.mainIdea: Hebrews 1 and 2 argue from the Hebrew Bible that the Son is greater than the angels.
reading: The letter to the Hebrews opens with an argument about angels. Hebrews 1:4 says the Son has become "so much better than the angels." Then the writer strings together quotations from the Hebrew Bible. Hebrews 1:5 asks to which angel God ever said, "Thou art my Son" (Psalm 2:7). Hebrews 1:14 calls angels "ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation."

Hebrews 1:6 says, "let all the angels of God worship him." This line is not in the standard Hebrew text of the Bible, the *Masoretic Text*. It matches Deuteronomy 32:43 in the *Septuagint*, the ancient Greek translation. A Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy found among the Dead Sea Scrolls has a similar line. Heiser often pointed to cases like this, where the New Testament follows an older form of the text.

Hebrews 2:7 quotes Psalm 8, where humans are made "a little lower than the angels." The Hebrew of Psalm 8:5 has elohim there, and the Septuagint rendered it angels. Hebrews 2:5 adds that the world to come is not put under angels. Heiser read these chapters as showing the Son's rank over the whole heavenly host. Most Christian readers agree with that main point. They differ on why the writer needed to argue it so strongly.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, preserved by Jewish scribes in the Middle Ages
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in the 200s BCE
Hebrews 1:14's description of angels as servants sent to help

look.title: Ministering Spirits
look.text: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?"
look.prompt: Is this verse describing what angels are, what they do, or both? Use the ideas of status words and role words.

check.q: Where does the line "let all the angels of God worship him" in Hebrews 1:6 come from?
check.why: The line matches the Greek Septuagint of Deuteronomy 32:43. A Dead Sea Scrolls copy has a similar Hebrew line.

check.q: In Psalm 8:5, which Hebrew word did the Septuagint translate as angels?
check.why: Psalm 8:5 in Hebrew has elohim. The Septuagint rendered it angels, and Hebrews 2:7 quotes that form.

check.q: What does Hebrews 1:14 call angels?
choices: Rulers of the world to come
check.why: Hebrews 1:14 calls them ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation.

review.q: Which pair shows Heiser's difference between a role word and a status word?
review.why: Messenger (mal'ak) names a job. Elohim names a being's home in the spirit world, a status.

review.q: Who sees seraphim calling "Holy, holy, holy" above the LORD's throne?
review.why: Isaiah 6 tells the prophet's vision of the seraphim in the year King Uzziah died.

review.q: How did Heiser read the "us" in Isaiah 6:8, and how do some other readers differ?
choices: He said it meant Isaiah and the king; others say the priests
He read it as God speaking before his council; others hear a royal way of speaking or a hint of the Trinity
He said it was a copying error; others say it is poetry
He said it meant the seraphim only; others say the people
review.why: Heiser read "us" as God addressing his council. Other readers hear a royal plural or, in many Christian readings, the Trinity.

review.q: Which beings guard the ark's cover in Exodus 25?
review.why: Exodus 25:18-22 describes two golden cherubim over the ark's cover.

review.q: The word watcher in Daniel 4 is Aramaic. Which later writing uses the same word for beings who sinned?
review.why: The Aramaic copies of 1 Enoch use 'irin for the Watchers who sinned. Daniel's watchers are faithful.

review.q: Which statement about the nine choirs of angels is accurate?
choices: They are listed in order in Colossians 1:16
They come from Pseudo-Dionysius, about 500 CE
review.why: The nine choirs come from The Celestial Hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius. Paul names some powers but gives no ranked list.

review.q: Which idea did Heiser call popular rather than biblical?
review.why: Heiser stressed that the Bible treats angels and humans as different kinds of beings. The dead do not become angels.

review.q: How does Hebrews 1 argue that the Son is greater than the angels?
choices: By telling a new vision of heaven
By quoting passages from the Hebrew Bible, some in their Septuagint form
review.why: Hebrews 1 builds its case from quotations such as Psalm 2:7 and Deuteronomy 32:43 in the Septuagint.
